description: We’re building SmogWatch: merging NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire data into a crop-burning calendar and AI forecast that warns when stubble fires will push smog into Lahore. I’m a CS grad with Python backend and ML experience. Looking for: a frontend/data-viz developer, someone who knows remote sensing or GIS, and a designer or storyteller to make our demo video. Remote, async-friendly. Let’s turn NASA data into cleaner air for millions.
summary:
SmogWatch is a public web app that merges NASA's MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one record of crop-residue burning across Punjab (Pakistan and India) and Haryana, the main source of Lahore's autumn smog.

We combined 1.97 million detections from five satellites (2012–2026) into a single format, mapped confidence onto one common scale, and merged repeat sightings of the same fire into 1.2 million fire events. From this record, the app builds a burning activity calendar with season start, peak and critical days. It also computes a Lahore Smoke Exposure Index, which uses NASA POWER wind data to show which fires actually send smoke toward the city.

Harmonizing the two sensors matters: 10% of fires were seen only by MODIS. Comparing years fairly matters too. Newer satellites inflate raw counts, and once we used the same satellites every year, burning was falling in India but rising in Pakistan.

This gives officials, schools and residents clear, early evidence of when and where burning threatens Lahore's air.
details:
What it does

SmogWatch is a public web app that turns NASA's two fire-detecting instruments, MODIS and VIIRS, into one trustworthy record of crop-residue burning across Punjab (Pakistan and India) and Haryana, and links that record to smoke over Lahore. It has five views:

  • Today: a map of fires from the last 2–14 days, filterable by satellite and country.
  • Burning Calendar: a year-by-day heatmap of every season since 2012, with season start, peak, end and critical days, plus a tool to compare years.
  • Why Combine Satellites?: evidence for why merging the instruments matters.
  • Smog Link: a daily Lahore Smoke Exposure Index, with a day-by-day lookup of wind and upwind fires.
  • About: method, data, limitations and a glossary.

How it works

  1. Fetch: an automated pipeline downloads NASA FIRMS active-fire data from five satellites (Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21). It uses archive data where available and near-real-time data for recent weeks, chosen automatically from FIRMS's data-availability service.
  2. Harmonize: both sensors go into one format, with confidence on a common scale (MODIS 0–100 and VIIRS low/nominal/high both become low/nominal/high). Low-confidence detections and known industrial heat sources are removed.
  3. De-duplicate: for each day, detections within 1 km are clustered (DBSCAN, haversine distance) into single fire events tagged MODIS-only, VIIRS-only or both. This turned 1.97 million detections into 1.20 million fires.
  4. Analyze: season statistics, critical days (above the 90th percentile for that time of year in earlier years only), and Mann-Kendall trend tests.
  5. Smoke Exposure Index: for each day, it takes fires within 300 km of Lahore that lie within ±45° of the direction the wind comes from (NASA POWER), weights fire intensity by distance, boosts calm and humid days, and scales the result to 0–100.

Key findings

  • 10% of fires were seen only by MODIS and 83% only by VIIRS. They pass at different times, and straw fires burn out quickly, so neither sensor alone is enough.
  • Newer satellites inflate raw counts: 2018 jumps 63% when NOAA-20 starts. With a constant set of satellites, burning is falling in India (p = 0.009) and rising in Pakistan (p = 0.003), with Pakistan's season starting earlier.

Benefits and intended impact

The app gives environment agencies (EPA Punjab, PDMA) evidence of where and when to enforce burning bans. Schools and district administrations get earlier warning of smoky days, residents get a plain-language daily smoke level, and researchers and journalists get a clean, de-duplicated record with country-level trends. It also shows that Lahore's smog is a shared, cross-border problem.

Creativity

Most fire maps answer "where are the fires?" SmogWatch answers "which fires are sending smoke to my city today?" We also found and corrected a hidden bias, the changing number of satellites, which reverses the conclusions about trends.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: every number can be reproduced from the code, and the app states its limits: detections are heat signals, not confirmed crop fires; clouds hide fires; and the index estimates smoke transport, not measured air quality.
  • Data integrity: days that were never downloaded are never shown as zero.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe colours, plain-language explanations on every chart, and a glossary.
  • Speed: the app reads small pre-computed files, so it loads quickly.

Tools

Python 3.13; pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (DBSCAN), pymannkendall, shapely, PyArrow/Parquet; Streamlit, Plotly and pydeck for the app; pytest (43 tests); Git/GitHub; Streamlit Community Cloud for hosting. No special hardware was used.
